utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have two decisions to give. The first one relates to the request by the Defence for the admission of 151 documents intended for use in the testimony of witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For witness T-35, Snezana Marinkovic Jekic. Among these documents, 62 were not translated at all and 14 only partially translated. In the hearing of the 19th of July, the parties made submissions on the admission of these documents. The Chamber, having considered the list of 151 documents, does not admit the following documents: 1D, 2D, 4D, 5D, 7D, 10D, 19D, 34D, 43D, 44D, 101D, and 135D. Additionally, the Chamber will not admit the 14 documents which are only partially translated, and those are numbers 165D to 167D, 170D, 171D, 173D to 178D, 186D, 195D, and 196D. Also it will not admit the 62 documents which are not translated at all from number 224D onwards until a complete translation is provided, at which time the Chamber will evaluate the relevance and probative value of these documents so as to determine their admissibility. The remaining documents are admitted. That's the first decision. The second decision relates to a motion filed by the Defence on the 20th of July for the admission into evidence of three witnesses. I should say, rather, three witness statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Defence requested protective measures for one of the three witnesses. On 24th July, the Prosecution informed the Court that it did not object either to the admission into evidence of the three witness statements or the requested protective measures. The Chamber has reviewed the statements of Witnesses T-20, T-40, and T-44. The statements meet the requirements of Rule 92 bis. There is no need for the witnesses to be called for cross-examination. The statements are admitted upon fulfilment of the certification procedure set out in Rule 92 bis B. The Defence requested the protective measures of pseudonym and image distortion for Witness T-20. In light of the decision on admission of the statements, the protective measure of image distortion will not be necessary. The protective measure of pseudonym will be granted and the statement of Witness T-20 is admitted, under seal. Those are the two decisions, and we may now continue with the hearing of evidence by calling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration. Make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. You may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. This is a protected witness. Has all the three forms of protective measures. Could he be shown document DD00-3987 in order that he may confirm that the document contains his first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can that document be admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we move into private session now, please, for some details concerning the witness's personal background and some other matters the witness will say at the outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could you tell us something -- could you tell us whether you were an eye-witness of anything that had to do with the way those hand-grenades were used in the area of responsibility controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I often saw the hand-grenades manufactured by me and my colleague being thrown into abandoned Serb homes in order to render those homes inhabitable. I often saw boys do that, 14-, 15-year-old boys, not older than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say that, you are talking about the whole period, from 1992 until the end of the war. You would see that occasionally, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us as you went to work, because from Vojnicko Polje to Pofalici you have to move towards the city centre, is that not so? You actually go towards the city centre, towards the Miljacka as you move in that direction. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many kilometres would that be in one direction? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: A bit more than four kilometres one way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In all those years - I have to dwell on this - so in all those years, I'm asking you to focus on just the most important things related to what I'm going to ask you about. Did you ever notice any heavy weapons in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes. Every day the artillery position at Alipasino Polje, which borders with Vojnicko Polje, my neighbourhood, would fire on Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to obtain a time-period, is the witness saying every day from 1992 to 1995 or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, what time-period do you have in mind, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1992 until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, but -- the complaint was that you said every day from 1992 to 1995, and I wish to find out whether you could be more specific, or do you mean literally every day from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not every day, but very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was about to clear this up. That's precisely what I wanted to ascertain, whether the witness could tell us something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if you say that, the way you just put it, did this fire that came from Alipasino Polje, was there any response to it from the Republika Srpska army positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska army responded only when those attacks of the BH army would get very frequent and incessant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But could you tell me, was there a period when there was no fire or perhaps there was fire, I don't want to put things in your mouth, that the Republika Srpska army did not fire at all from its heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska army weapons stopped firing sometime in 1994, and they remained silent until the very end of 1994. And then in 1995, when the BH army really launched those frequent attacks from all positions within the city of Sarajevo, in 1995, the Serb artillery started responding to those attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in 1995, in this time-period that you just described, you were in Sarajevo, you were able to hear or to see or just to hear or just to see, you will explain that if anyone wants you to, this fire, and you felt it, just as you were able to hear, see, and feel the response of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes. Those activities were particularly intensified in this area where I lived. From Alipasino Polje the fire doubled in volume in relation to the previous year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were there any cases when we're talking about this fire that was opened from Alipasino Polje, how far is Vojnicko Polje from Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Vojnicko Polje is 100 metres from Alipasino Polje, just the road leading to Lukavica divides the two. So very often, as they fired over the buildings where I lived, they would hit those buildings where I lived, the Federation buildings. So that many apartments, and my apartment for one, were damaged more from the side where BH army had its positions than from the side where the Serb army had its positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This part of the apartment that was hit was facing which positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: My apartment was facing both Serb positions and the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will be showing you a photograph later. But I'm interested in one other aspect of this and then we will not be dealing with it anymore. When you went into town at the time when you didn't work, did you go into town at the times when you didn't work and why? When I say "town," I mean downtown, the centre of the city that was controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I went into town to see my doctor, as I was on sick-leave. I could see and I assert that because I was able to see that and I saw that, that every day the cannon out of the general area where the hospital was fired upon the Serb positions, and mostly so on the neighbourhood of Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say "every day." Can you tell us how often you passed through that area, if you can?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record, I'd like to know which hospital. I assume counsel is going to get to that. Which hospital the witness is talking about, and in my submission, there was no -- there was no mention of this evidence in the 65 ter summary and I understand that the witness was speaking about the area he lived in and the area he worked in. I understand the ruling that Your Honours have given that it is supposed to be a summary. However, this evidence is -- is important in terms of my preparation for cross-examination, I would submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me explain this. He lived in that town, and to go to work he would go through the centre of town. Of course in one's lifetime there are several stages, a person falls ill and then of course the summary does state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Go ahead. You say the summary does state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The summary talks about this fact, that he lived in Sarajevo in the BH army-controlled area of the town, and that he can testify to all the matters he witnessed throughout the war. What else can I put there? Unless I was required to state in detail all the experiences he had and all the sufferings he felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we still don't know what hospital it is, to answer to the question of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him answer that question and then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I put the question to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us what hospital this was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the military hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you yourself, Witness, by either hearing or seeing? Let me not put words into your mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for pursuing this. But if I understand it, the military hospital, at least in this case, evidence has been lead that the military hospital is indeed the State Hospital in Sarajevo. Perhaps that can be clarified. And if indeed that is the case, then the Prosecution has led evidence that the State Hospital was targeted by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and this evidence-- this potential evidence now from this witness is, in my submission, important or at least requires more preparation on my part for cross-examination. It is a significant issue, I would submit and this was not mentioned in the 65 ter summary. And this is given the understanding of Your Honour's ruling, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So are you not in a position then to -- to question the witness about the targeting of the hospital by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can, of course. However it may be that I might -- I might have to add some exhibits that I had not anticipated for my cross and if that is the case, I would ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, when we come to that, if -- you will have, I believe, the benefit of the break, so you may be deprived of coffee and croissant, but all in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this slight break we had, I noticed omitting something. You said that you observed that the fire coming out of town was responded to from the positions held by the Serb army. Your neighbours, you and all the people living around you, how did they experience, how did they take in all these events, if you can tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: All the citizens took this -- it was very hard upon them. But so it was for all the sides. The Serb population had particular difficulties taking this in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say the Serb population. Which Serb population? The Serbs who lived in the area where you weren't present throughout the war, or the Serb population that happened to be in the areas controlled by the 1st Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: When I said the Serb population, I meant the Serb population present in the Federation, because those are the ones I know something about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I had not ask you about any possible victims on the Serb sides. Let me ask you this: As a result of all the fighting and fire in Sarajevo, were there casualties, and primarily I mean civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: It is only natural that when there's a war on, there are victims and there were victims on the Federation side too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this, briefly, please: Did you witness the fire being opened from that cannon in the vicinity of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us in what direction the cannon fired, but can you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: It fired upon the neighbourhood of Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In those situations when you were able to observe this, did the Serb side respond to this fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: There was a response, only in such situations when heavy artillery fired upon the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, but I'd like to know the time-frame, when was this observed, what did he see. I can ask this in cross, but it would assist me in my preparation if these answers are forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What time-frame is this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military hospital formerly, now the State Hospital, is less than one kilometre away from my factory. You can see the general perimeter and the hospital buildings from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I want to find out is, following upon the submission the Prosecutor, was when did this occur, what time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the year or in -- during the way, which part of the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, be as specific as you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went on sick-leave in mid-1994, every seven days I would go to my doctors for a checkup. On my way there, I had to pass by the military hospital. Almost every day the cannon positioned in the perimeter of the hospital fired. I even saw fire being opened upon Serb positions as I was going past the hospital. It happened in day-time. It may have been 10.00 or 11.00 a.m. when I was on my way to the doctors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the year 1994. You said something about the events of that year. But was the situation the same in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else now. While you were working, before you went on sick-leave, were you ever in a position enabling you to be absent from work, because, as you said yourself, you were quite exhausted, and you had to work 12 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we move into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness mentioned the place where he worked. Can that part of the transcript be redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you've already told us, can you tell us what sort of treatment were you meted out during the time you worked there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: While I started working there in 1992, both physical and psychological mistreatment began. What sort of mistreatment or abuse was this. Quite often I would be intercepted on my way home and taken to the places where civilians or victims were placed, that they had treated or done something with during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to go through this briefly, please. Can you tell us the most radical forms of it, what was it that you experienced most often, and then you can perhaps give us an example of it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I was taken away during my work there on 11 occasions. The most drastic example occurred in early November of 1992, when I was stopped at 2000 p.m. as I was on my way home. I was placed in a black van and taken somewhere. It was night-time and it was dark. I was thrown out of the van and taken to a ditch or a pit where a massacre had been committed during the day. I will not exaggerate if I say that more than 20 mutilated maimed bodies were there. I can't even express that in words, but this is something that leaves me sleepless at night. I saw a child whose head had been cut off and placed on his mother's chest. His hands had been cut off and -- or his arms had been cut off and placed on the child's chest in the form of a cross. They through me into that pit where I lost consciousness, I fainted. I don't know how long I was in there, but when I came to, they placed me in that van again, drove me some 200 metres further down from that place --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Let us not dwell on this point any longer. Can you tell us whether they told you why this was being done to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: They told me, swearing my Serb mother, You see what fate will befall you unless you go to work and work even harder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that this happened 11 times. When did this happen for the last time, if you can? Let us just hear the date without going into details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: The last time it happened it was in August of 1994, when, again, I was placed in a black van where there were four persons who had been tied up. I was taken somewhere in the territory of Pofalici, and before my very eyes all of the four people were shot to death. They threatened me that the same thing would happen to me the following day unless I went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you were on sick-leave at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, I was on sick-leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's DD00-1861. So could we look at it, and -- the photograph and then I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read what this is, slowly as you do, from the top to the bottom. There's not too much information here. Could you please read it. But read it aloud, please. Could you just read the heading, what it says in the middle of the document and the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: You mean here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Do read what is in this document the way I just instructed you. Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: "The republic Bosnia-Herzegovina staff of the supreme command of the armed forces security administration, defence of the republic, military secret, strictly confidential, copy number -- to be returned" -- well, I can't really read this because of the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: "Special report."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the date down there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: The date is the 17th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at just one excerpt, whether this corresponds to what you just described to us. That's at page four. It's also page four in the English version. And when you have that in front of you, in order to save some time, could you please start reading from where it says -- it's actually page 5 in the B/C/S version and 4 in the English version. That's first paragraph, and then you can see here it is about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: "This concerns crimes against humanity and international law, Article 142 of the penal code, perpetrated against the civilian population, murders committed in a particularly vicious manner, torture and inflicting great suffering, given that most of the crimes were according to the information obtained so far committed against Serbs, they even take on elements of genocide."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at the last page to see who signed this, because it is a Federation document dated 1993. If you look at the bottom, you will see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: It was signed by Jusuf Jasarevic, chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that correspond to what you just told us and I didn't want you to tell us everything, all the other things. Does that correspond, this the cruelty the viciousness, does this tally with what you told us about this pit that you were thrown in? So does that tally with your account, in terms of torture, murder, viciousness which they themselves state in their report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it really does. It's as if I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted as a Defence exhibit. It's DD00-1861.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lest there should be any misunderstandings, you gave us your decision a little while ago -- just a moment, please. Yes, it was not admitted when it was on the list that you had in front of you, but I'm now tendering it. You gave us your decision, and according to the information that I have, it has not been admitted but after this evidence of -- by an eye-witness who told us what he had been through, I tender it into evidence. Of course, Mr. Sachdeva can state his views and we can hear what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the admission of this document. The witness has given evidence concerning one allegation, one incident and this document, as I understand it, is nine pages long. So the question as to whether it tallies with this document, frankly in my submission, is -- does not get us anywhere and therefore I can't see how tendering this complete document, this report of nine pages through this witness on the basis of one incident that the witness has spoken about merits the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But we could admit it in relation to that one incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps if the document refers to the incident the witness speaks about. But Mr. Tapuskovic pointed the witness to a particular paragraph that was, in my submission, general. It spoke about allegations of genocide and torture, and accentuated the sufferings of Serbs but there is no relation to the specific incident that the witness spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to bother you. I didn't want to bother you, because God save us from this witness telling us all those things that he had been through. I didn't want to put you in that situation, but on page 5 or 6 of this very same document I didn't want to force him to read that out. That's on page 7 in the English version where it says that some commanders forced their own people, that's according to the report, to-- they would -- he is the commander but he would force his subordinate, in order to get him involved in that, to commit such murders. I could read five more paragraphs. That's all in this document. But I don't want to bother you with this. I just gave you an example, and it is stated here that this was done solely for retaliation. I don't know, Your Honours, whether you admitted this document through Snezana Marinkovic Jekic perhaps, but this does constitute grounds for the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, again for the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps indeed if this document has been admitted in the earlier ruling of the Chamber then this discussion is -- is redundant. However, Mr. Tapuskovic now mentions another example and again I don't see the reference to the evidence the witness has given. It is all in very general terms. The witness has not made any mention of commanders or who in fact took him in the van. So I can't see the relation between the witness's evidence and the specific examples Mr. Tapuskovic refers to. And therefore I persist in my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm checking with the clerk to see whether we have admitted it or have not admitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll reserve our ruling on this until we have carried out the check. Continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will -- in light of Mr. Sachdeva' intervention I will have to ask you the following question. I didn't mean to ask you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you see on one occasion on the door of an orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption of my learned counsel, but my case manager has informed me that the document is 131D, Defence Exhibit 131 and I understand from the ruling that -- Your Honour's ruling that it has indeed been admitted. Perhaps the Defence could check that, but that's what -- that's the information I have from my case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If indeed it is 131D, then it has been admitted because it is not included in the list of those not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this document discusses precisely the kind of things that this witness talked about and the kind of cruelty, I didn't want to dwell on it, but in light of Sachdeva's intervention, I really have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, what did you see -- precisely to testify to one thing that is very important and relevant for the lives of the people. I want to ask you were only Serbs the ones who suffered in this way or were killed in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You are not to proceed until I have made up my mind as to whether I'm going to allow to you ask the question. You don't run these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that. I don't know if there's anyone who has more respect for you than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, there is no need to ask the witness any further questions. And the document, it has been admitted. We can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, you -- I assure you that I have utmost respect for you and I'm not asking anything out of any kind of spite. This witness is testifying about some things that very important for your final deliberations. I am not in a position to ask any further questions. I asked him, and I believe that I can ask him to tell us about something that he saw at one place at the orthodox church in the very heart of Sarajevo. I can ask him that, and I think that you should allow me to do so. If you disallow it, then of course I will not ask the question and I am absolutely -- I know that you run the proceedings, and I never doubted that in any way, and I always abided by your rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The answer is no. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let us now deal with this place where you lived. This will be very relevant, and the Trial Chamber really needs to look at a document 65 ter 2862. But we have to move into private session because we will be talking about the witness's apartment and we will be dealing it until the end of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And perhaps I could ask the court officer to bring up the D352 under seal and not for it to be broadcast, so I can try and do this in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: T-60, I'm just waiting for the photograph that you marked to be brought up, and without mentioning where you lived I just wanted to ask a clarification question to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm waiting for the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, as I understand it, your evidence is that in buildings 1 or the set of buildings in 1, 2 and 3, your evidence is that no civilians lived there throughout the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, of course, the building where you lived, there were civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And one of the questions from counsel for the Defence asked you -- and I'm -- part of the question is: I'm asking you whether in the building where you lived and in the building to the left of number 1, were there any civilians there, and your answer was yes. And I'd just like you to circle the building left of number 1. That's at least how the answer is transcribed -- the question is transcribed, rather.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so in that building, civilians lived there throughout the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: The buildings that I circled, before I made this circle right now, I said that there were no civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The blue circle, sir, is where civilians lived throughout the conflict, is that right, and if it is, can you put the number 6 there, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: No, that -- you wanted me to circle the building to the left of number 1. I did so. But I didn't say that there were civilians there. I circled it first with a red pen, indicating that there were no civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, we have a slight confusion because I'm trying to establish which other building apart from the building you lived in you say civilians lived. And the question -- I'll repeat the full question from counsel. "Then you didn't understand my question. You told us what you had to tell us concerning the buildings circled 1, 2, and 3. Your building is behind item 2 and then there were other buildings around. I'm asking you whether in the building where you lived and in the building to the left of number 1, were there any civilians living there." And you answered yes. So, Witness T-60, I'm trying to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Tapuskovic on his feet. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's the whole confusion. To the left of the building marked with 1 there's no building. There are no buildings to the left of the building marked with 1, so I can't understand how the question can refer to an area to the left of the building marked with number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm reading verbatim from counsel's question. And that's why -- that's indeed why I started off with this question because I myself don't see the buildings that witness or counsel speaks about. If one looks at page 38, line 13 to 18, therein lies the question and therein lies the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Line what? Which line on page 38?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's page 38 and it's line 13 to 18 and it's the last component of the question which reads: "I'm asking whether you in the building where you lived and in the building to the left of number 1 were there any civilians there," and the answer was yes. So I'm trying to establish which building the witness speaks about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he has marked a building in blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so I did -- I assume then that was the building. However, the witness has now said that no civilians lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this can only be an error in translation and nothing else because witness marked this building with number 1 and I asked him to the left of his building, the building where he lived. And then he gave his explanation. If we are now going to be sticking to something that I'm sure was a lapse, because I know for a fact that I asked him about the building to the left of where he lived after he had already marked the building with another building with number 1, so this kind of examination is really is objectionable. This could be nothing else but a rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the mark signifying the building where he lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's marked with the letter K and I asked him to the left of that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, when you were asked to mark the building to the left of the building where you lived, or asked about that building, what building did you have in mind? Can you show us on the -- on this chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the left of the building where I live, I was asked to circle it and I circled this row of buildings where there were no civilians. To the left of my building, behind number 1, the second row of buildings, that's where the civilians were. I don't know why I was asked to circle the building to the left of number 1, which I did. I don't know what the purpose was that -- was of that, since this building had already been circled in red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you understand now, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do now, and just to allay the concerns of counsel I simply repeated what was transcribed and that's why I myself had confusion so there was nothing untoward in my seeking clarification. But it is now understand now. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we should then delete the blue circle which marks a building, since it evidently doesn't represent what was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness T-60, you said earlier today that in the area marked 1, 2, and 3 you -- throughout the time you lived in that area, you never ventured -- you never ventured in the area, in the vicinity of 1, 2, and 3. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I never ventured to building number 3. Now, as for building number 2, it's opposite my building. It's maybe 20 metres away from my building. And the building to the left of my building on the other side of the road leading to Alipasino Polje, I went there every day, and I was able to observe what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So then when Mr. Tapuskovic asked you if you went into the area in the vicinity of 1, 2 and 3, it's not totally correct. You did in fact venture into the area in front of the buildings marked with 1 and 2. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, I had to. I had to pass through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he said to the left of his building, towards the building to the left of his building, not towards building marked with 1. You can ask him again. He went behind this towards this other building. You can ask him again. It was quite clearly stated. He never said that he went in the area of front of building 1 but he did say that he was walking or going in the other -- on the other side. That is the essence of what he said and it is actually recorded here, that he moved behind the building marked with number 1 just as he was able to move in front of his building that is marked with letter K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you this: Concentrate on the buildings marked 1, 2, and 3. And on the photograph you will see in front of each of those buildings, in other words, towards the bottom of the photograph there are open areas. You see that, sir, in 1, 2, and 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what I'm asking you is, that during the conflict, in other words 1992 to 1995, did you ever venture in those areas, in front of those buildings, towards the bottom of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: No. The open area that can you see, that's where those communal garages were and they were always full of troops. This area that you can see in front of number 2 and number 1, that's the communal garages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, of course, you never saw that, did you, because you never went there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I saw building 2 from the side that's facing my building, because, as I said, it is maybe about 20 metres. You can talk to each other. People could talk to each other if they stood on the balconies and as for building number 1, that -- there where this open area is, this is not where I went. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me try -- I'm sorry to persist on this, because I'm not understanding your evidence. If we look at 1, 2, and 3 and we look at the areas -- in other words the areas on the other side towards the bottom of the photograph, the open areas in front of the complex number 1, in front of complex number 2 and in front of complex number 3, the areas towards the bottom of the photograph, I understand that you never visited that area during the conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so my question is: If you did not go to those areas, you did not see the troops that you spoke about, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. From my building, I had to go out, if you look at this place where the letter K is, that's a small alley dividing those two buildings. That's my street. I had to get out here where I am marking with my pen to continue on towards the sky-scrapers at Alipasino Polje. I had to go every day down that route as I went to work and back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just point the small alley-way. The small alley dividing the buildings, could you just identify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then, Witness, from that marking that you just made I understand that you went towards the top of the photograph. That's the route you took towards 4 and 5. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please continue with the blue line and draw that route.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the building number 1, you see the building number 1? I want you to place a cross just beneath the number 1, the figure number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And would you please do the same for the building in number 2 and in number 3. Place a cross just beneath the figures.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my understanding is that where those crosses are -- where you have placed those crosses, those are the places you never visited throughout the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: That's right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so you never saw troops that were in those locations, if indeed they were, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Sir, I could see the troops as I passed through here, between those two buildings here, and I -- as I went out into the street, outside of my doorway, and also when I went out into the street that runs through my neighbourhood, leading towards Alipasino Polje, even before I went to this area marked with the cross, because the troops were always walking down these areas in their hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You never saw the troops firing from those buildings, did you, if indeed they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I can't say that I saw that, but gun-fire can be felt. I was trying to move along that area quite quickly, so that one of their lot wouldn't shoot me to death. I was called a Chetnik every day. I had rifles or, rather, pistols in my face and knives under my chin, threats against my life whilst I was producing 120 hand-grenades for their purposes every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just clarify that. You said that you were threatened while you were producing what you were producing. So I take it you were threatened at the area where you were working and not -- not in the area where you were living; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was being threatened --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just have something redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was threatened at my doorstep night and day. They'd come over. On several occasion whenever I was late for work for whatever reason, they came to see where I was, to check up on me, so that I might not go somewhere and report them. Whenever I was at the workplace, everything was fine. I wasn't bothered with this. All of this happened outside my workplace. If you will allow me to tell you this as well. Behind number 5 there, I was stopped there on several occasion. There was a prison there of their commander, somebody mentioned earlier on that there were some commanders involved. There was the commander of the special forces of the BH army there, Luka Prasina, who was released by Alija Izetbegovic from prison and who was appointed there by him. This was his private prison. They would take me there in order to force me to watch what they were doing to the prisoners. They would bring out these half dead people, and they would bring this dog, a shepherd who was well-fed, to mistreat them and then they'd tell me, Unless you're at Vase Miskina factory in 20 minutes time, this is what you will see happening to you tonight. This is what somebody told me in my own neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: There is what Luka Prasina told me in my own neighbourhood. In 1992 and in 1993 on several occasions. Because I had to pass by the building where his prison was every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the date, sir, of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember the date when -- when you saw, as you said, dead people and dogs were mistreating dead people. You don't remember those dates, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, if I can say, I recall that on that earlier incident when they took me to see that pit, that was on the 27th of October, 1992. I wanted to write about that, but then they searched my flat and they found some pieces of paper where they said I had noted down some of the dates, and after this happened I no longer wrote about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what was the date when you saw the dog?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't once that I saw it. I saw it dozens of times. There would be people coming out -- into their balconies and looking in the direction of the prison, as if it were a theatre or any -- or entertainment of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I take it that you lived in that area from 1992 through to the end of the conflict, is that right, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I lived there until 1996, when they came and ordered me. They told me, If you want to stay alive and you do deserve to stay alive because you worked for us, so if you want to stay alive, leave the premises tomorrow morning, and I did that. I called a friend of mine to take me away, to help me to go away. They threw this friend of mine later on out of his apartment and allowed a man who had two more houses to move into his flat. You have to hear this out. I returned and then I asked him, Why did they give you this flat if you already have two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am sorry to interrupt you, but we don't have much time. I would just like you to stick to the questions I'm asking you. You lived in the area throughout the conflict, and if I understand you correctly, in 1994, sometime in the middle of 1994, you started seeking medical attention. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you mind if I ask you what -- what particular ailment did you have? Can I do that in open session, or would you like me to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let the witness answer. Do you want it to be in private session, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer right now. As they were throwing me into that pit with the corpses, my arm broke, and I couldn't do anything about it. I continued working with my arm as it was fractured. I was also hit, or, rather, I received a blow against my spine and the result of this was that I was prone to fainting. My arm hurt me very much. And I worked for some five or six months with the hand thus fractured, and as I started losing consciousness on a frequent basis I went to see this Croat doctor who placed me on sick-leave and treated me until I was expelled from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the incident with the pit was in October 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you started seeking medical attention in June 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're aware as was everyone living in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time that there was a conflict that unfortunately ravaged the country. You're aware of that, aren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you're also aware that unfortunately one of the -- one of the results of this conflict was that there were population displacements, in other words people for whatever reason had to leave their residences, from all over the country.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I can only speak for myself. I know that I was driven out. I wasn't a refugee. I was expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, you're aware that Croats and Muslims and Serbs would leave their municipalities where they lived and move into the cities, move in to Banja Luka, to Sarajevo, Tuzla. That happened, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where are you going with this, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, I'm moving towards the evidence about the civilians living in -- or not living in the flats. But I will do it in a quicker fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, as you have testified you lived in Sarajevo during the conflict, you must have been aware of the influx of civilians and persons moving to the city during -- during that time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know who was moving in. I spent very little time at home. I spent my time at work. I only used my time at home to sleep for a few hours, as far as I was able to, what, with all the gun-fire. And to go back to work. It's not that I worked for 12 hours only. I used to work for 15 hours or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you worked up until June 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, after June 1994, you lived in your flat, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you worked at the place where you worked, and now you've said you worked for 15 hours, of course while you were there at work you did not and could not see any military activity if indeed was some in the area where you lived; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the evidence that you've given with respect to the -- the artillery fire you said that emanated from Alipasino Polje was from the balance of nine hours in the day that you spent at that place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, as far as Alipasino Polje is concerned, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, those flats in circles 1, 2, 3 and indeed the flat where you lived, I take it there were about 11 floors in each of those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many floors were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Seven and eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many flats on each floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Four flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, did you live with your family there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, with my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the complex where you lived, how many sets of seven-floor buildings were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: The entire neighbourhood of Vojnicko Polje had buildings of seven or eight floors each.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But if we look at the circle number 1, is it correct that there are about four or five such buildings with seven floors in a row? Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just take circle number 1. You'll see that there is a row of buildings. And what I'm asking you is that how many rows comprised that set of buildings and therefore how many seven-storey building complexes were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps one can count them on this photograph. But I don't know. I didn't count them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you would agree that there is at least five.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take the building that you lived in. There were seven storeys and on each storey there was four flats, four residential spaces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you agree that each flat, the average household would contain four persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, generally you would agree that there is typically a mother and a father and some children. So on average, I'm not asking whether it is specific to these buildings, but on average, a household would contain four persons. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know. My household consisted of two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you agree, sir, that in the complex where you lived in, there would have been space for approximately at least over 250 persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking to agree to anything that's controversial. The flats, as you've said, have seven storeys and each storey has four flats on them. And so my question is simply that there would have at least been space -- I'm not saying that there were, but there would have at least been space for over 250 people. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know. It is possible that you can fit seven or eight people in an apartment such as mine, which had an area of 55 square metres, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So therefore it is possible in the buildings where you lived in and also in 1, 2 and 3 for well over 250 persons to live in those buildings. You'll agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: It is possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to try and quickly finish with this exercise. So what I'm suggesting to you, sir, is that the buildings marked 1, 2 and 3, you would agree that in total there was the potential to house at least 750 to 1.000 persons, there was that potential, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an answer to that, sir, because that would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, I'm not asking you to give me a precise figure. I'm asking you simply that there was a potential, given your evidence of the number of stories and the number of flats on each storey that in buildings 1, 2, 3 there was a potential to house over 750 persons. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm allowing the reformulation of the question. Witness, do you agree with what counsel has put to you, that based on the evidence that you have given, there was a potential for the buildings, the storeys and the flats in buildings 1, 2 and 3 to house over 750 persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it -- there was a potential for ten people to be at my place, and as of 1994, I have lived alone in my apartment, so I can't really speculate. If that is so, then let somebody confirm that this is indeed a potential situation. I can't tell you how many tenants there were and how many tenants could be, could fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You must move on now, Mr. Sachdeva, to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just one last question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Enough on that subject. That has been sufficiently ventilated. You do have a little tendency, Mr. Sachdeva, to overdo it. I think we have -- we have explored that one sufficiently, and then you're going to have Mr. Tapuskovic rising up when he should be resting himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just -- just as the Prosecution is under an obligation to put its case, I would just like to suggest to the witness that in buildings 1, 2, and 3, civilians lived there throughout the conflict, whether he agrees with that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that can be put. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll just put this question again to you. I suggest to you, sir, that in buildings 1, 2, and 3, during the conflict civilians indeed lived there. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I spent the war there, and I can be certain when I say that there were no civilians there. In buildings 1 and 2 there were no civilians. As for building 3, it was destroyed completely, so I can be sure that there were no civilians there, although I did not pass by that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. And in fact you never went to buildings 1, 2, and 3, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I've told you that. As for building number 2, I was able to talk to the neighbours who lived there from my balcony. I could see that. I could also see building number 1 as I went to work. I could see what people were doing there. I didn't have to go right there to do so, and as for the building number 3, I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you say you were able to talk to neighbours in building number 2, I take it, therefore, that civilians did live in building number 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I said that I could have, that there was no need for me to go there, but I saw the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So when you say you were speaking to your neighbours, you were saying that you were speaking to the troops in number 2, or what are you saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Judge Robinson, the witness said quite clearly it would -- I was able to talk to, had there been anyone there, he didn't say that he talked to civilians. He said had there been any civilians, he would have been able to talk to them. It's a very clear idea, this model, I was able to or I could have spoken to civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At line 5, page 62 says, "I was able to talk to the neighbours who lived there from my balcony," and therefore I understand counsel to be asking him who were these neighbours that you were able to speak to, were they military people or were they civilians. No? This is what is on our transcript. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's -- then it is not a correct translation of what the witness said. He said "I could have talked to" or "I could talk to neighbours." Well, I'm not the interpreter but I can tell you what it means when you say "I could." That's what he repeated, "I could if there were any neighbours." That's what he said, so perhaps he can then complete. "I could." He didn't say "I did." He said "I could." Because there were no neighbours or troops. There were no neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to have this one correct, you know, to find out what actually was said by the witness because there is a big difference between I talked to and I could have talked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But why would he be saying "I could have talked to neighbours"? Why would he be saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it's 20 metres away. In normal times, when you live a normal life, I was able to talk to people from my balcony in normal times. I could talk to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to see how best to resolve this. I would like to have it resolved. I don't think there's much point asking the witness now, because the issue has been ventilated. But let me ask him. Witness, what did you say and then I will have it -- I will have the translation done by the official unit. What did you actually say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about how close building number 2 was. It was so close that I was able to see and I was able, because it was so close, to talk to my neighbour, and if I had talked to my neighbours, I would have said I talked to them. That's what I meant. It is so close that you can talk to somebody who is in the other building from your window, if that person is on the window too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, we'll have to proceed on the basis of that answer for the time being, but I'm going to ask the translation unit to provide us with a translation as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my last -- my last question on this issue, in this case, we had a person that came here and testified, as you have done, as you are doing, a civilian who lived in the buildings marked number 1, and he was there throughout the conflict. And so now I'm asking you again, do you still maintain your evidence that no civilians lived in buildings number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I am not changing the answer that I have just given you. I lived there, and I didn't see any civilians there. And this building is close to where I was and I was able to see it without going there, and I said that I hadn't gone there, and I said that I hadn't seen any civilians there during the war. I saw civilians in civilian -- people in civilian clothes, but they were armed. They had rifles slung over their shoulders. Now if you consider these people to be civilians, then, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you went to work you would take that route that you have marked in blue. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the areas marked 4 and 5, those buildings were in Alipasino Polje, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you are aware that in front of those buildings there were small playgrounds or small parks that children and other persons could utilise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, indeed, when possible, children and other persons did use those spaces, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my question was that: Indeed, when it was possible, children and other persons did use those spaces, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: This space was an empty space, because there were some swings, that was a playground, and people took all those things away if they were made of wood to use as fuel. So these were empty spaces. The only exception would be if people behind those sky-scrapers at Alipasino Polje, people would go out and play football in those empty areas because all the other implements that there were at the children's playgrounds had already been taken away. Everything that was made of plastic or of wood had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And sir, during your time in that area, in other words throughout the conflict, you must have been aware or you must have heard or in fact even seen an incident in the winter of 1994, in January of 1994, where six children were killed while sledging in the snow in front of those buildings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I have never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No one of told you, you never saw anything in the media about that incident, an incident where you would pass -- an incident in a place where you would pass every day? Is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm saying. This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, yet, sir, you're able to give evidence about ABiH artillery fire from that area; in fact, quite detailed evidence and yet you can't talk about this incident. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I am speaking about things that I saw, and I don't want to speak about things that somebody may have told me about and nobody has told me about this. I'm only telling you about things that I saw or that I went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you can tell us about things that you have heard. That is -- that's permissible. So if you have heard about this incident, even if you haven't seen it with your eyes, you may tell us. You may tell us about it. So have you heard? Did you hear of this incident where six children were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I swear I have never heard about it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you started going to the hospital, the state hospital, that was in June 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you go to the hospital from the beginning, from that period, from June 1994 through to November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I have to make a correction here. I didn't go to the military hospital which is now the State Hospital but as I went to the Kosevo Hospital to receive treatment, I had to pass in front of the State Hospital, and I passed by this building every seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So your treatment was at the Kosevo Hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, not at the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it's correct, is it not, sir, that the State Hospital is some distance away from the Kosevo Hospital. In fact more than a kilometre. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I was to show you a map would you be able to mark the location of the Kosevo Hospital and the State Hospital, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, if it's there, if it is marked there, then I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 65 ter 02872 to be brought up, please. And perhaps I can tender this photograph into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P915, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, for the moment, can the map not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, while that map is being brought up, can you please answer how many times did you go to -- now you're saying the Kosevo Hospital for treatment from June 1994 through to November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, I would have to calculate this. As I said, I went there for the checkup every seven days, which would mean four times a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so I want to establish so from the period June through to November 1994, you went every seven days to the Kosevo Hospital continuously; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What time would you set off and what time would you reach the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, at a normal pace it would take me about one and a half hour. At that time it took me longer because I could barely walk. So about two hours, from my home to the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what time would your appointment be at the hospital, what time would you reach the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I always went there in the mornings, before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could have the map enlarged, please. Now, sir, I would like to you use a pen, and I'd like to you draw the route that you took from your place to the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: My flat is somewhere here. So here's Alipasino Polje. And the route towards the town was the yellow -- yellow line that can you see, Cengic Vila, the municipality of Novo Sarajevo and then I move forwards towards the city, Marindvor, and the State Hospital is at Marindvor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have to ask the witness to start marking where he started.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can barely see. It's really difficult to see things here on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the map be enlarged?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, it needs to be ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can't see it now, yeah. Are we going to start over?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Scroll down a little bit, please. No, no, that's fine, if you just -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, now please draw the route that you took.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I really can barely see. It was a bit bigger and I was able to see. Now it is a little bit more difficult. I said that Vojnicko Polje is somewhere here. So I went to Alipasino Polje. From Alipasino Polje, I get to this main road, leading from Ilidza to the city centre. That's Mese Selimovica Bulevar. I go to Cengic Vila, I move straight on to Marindvor, and from Marindvor I take a right -- a left turn here to cut my route shorter, right here in front of the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I mean Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why Mr. Sachdeva is not asked to instruct the witness to mark this whole route, just as he started marking because it is it obvious that the markings -- there are no markings. It is very useful for us to get the whole of the route, for the witness to mark the whole of the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I was about to do that once the witness had finished. Of course, that was my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please mark that route, the route that you have just described, please mark it with the red pen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in a little bit, because I can't read anything that's up there from Marindvor. I will start here. This is where my house is. I cross through Alipasino Polje. I go out to the Mese Selimovica Bulevar and then I take this road, and I pass through Cengic Vila. Otok is first, then Cengic Vila, and then we get to Marindvor. And now from this yellow line, which marks the main road, I take a left turn into a small street, it's a shortcut because I need to get to this yellow road here and I have to pass by the State Hospital here. I have to pass in front of the State Hospital to get this shortcut. Now I can't see a thing here. I get to this road here, and -- and the Kosevo Hospital is here. And that's it. Yes, this is where the Kosevo Hospital is. That's the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, when you took this route, as you said, every seven days, when you passed the State Hospital, I take it you -- you spent less than five minutes passing that hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And sometimes even -- even a shorter amount of time. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Sometimes even more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it your evidence, sir, that on those occasions while you passed the State Hospital on to Kosevo this is where you saw the cannon being fired. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many times, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
