utterances.text: Well, I didn't count. At least 20 times. I don't want to exaggerate. But at least some 20 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was it -- well, let me ask you. How many floors did the State Hospital have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know how many floors it had at that time. Now it has 20 floors, but at that time it was a smaller building, just a few floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So at the time of the conflict how many floors did it have, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't want to lie. But if -- I believe the State Hospital didn't have more than five floors. Although I'm not certain. I repeat that I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So when you say five, it could be less than five or it could be more than five?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, there were more and less than five, because the State Hospital didn't consist of one building only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's right, the State Hospital had more than one building, but the tallest building of that complex, how many floors would say you say it had, sir, during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know, and I don't want to say something that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, you passed that hospital every seven days for over a year, and you're telling the Court you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I have been going across Alipasino Polje for 25 years now and I still don't know what the highest sky-scraper there is, although I pass there every day. And there's a sky-scraper 50 metres away from my window, but I simply am not interested in looking at these details. Had I been lingering there counting how many floors there were, I would have been shot at, because somebody would mistake me for a Chetnik trying to obtain intelligence and pass it over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, I take it that after all these years, it's not easy to remember all the details, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Again, I'm going to play a role that interpreters don't enjoy, but here we really have an error, and I would like you to ask the CLSS to check the audiotape of what was said on line -- page 72, line 23, and -- to page 73, line 4. This is a very important answer provided by the witness, and I really believe that the interpretation is not accurate and does not reflect what was said, and defence submits that this might be very detrimental to its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You didn't read out the line, but are you referring then to the line which in English says "because somebody would mistake me for a Chetnik trying to obtain intelligence."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. There were many mistakes, not deliberate, of course, but I believe this must be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But before asking for it to be corrected, I should at least have an idea of the mistake. I can't just ask for something to be corrected because you have asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can tell you what the witness actually said. He did not say that someone could take him for a Chetnik, but -- well, I can't check -- speak French and check the interpretation at the same time. It's very difficult to do all these things at once. I don't know if what I'm saying is correctly interpreted at the moment. But he said that someone could have thought that he was providing information to the Chetniks by giving the positions where a cannon was shot from. And this changes everything. This is a very different thing than what can be read in -- what was translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll ask the CLSS to provide us with a translation of that line. The court deputy will ensure that that is done. And also the other matter that I referred to earlier. And I hope we'll get a response very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you when you went to the hospital, the Kosevo Hospital and when you passed the State Hospital, and where you said would you not linger, what time of day was that that you would pass the State Hospital roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I've already said that, around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it at that moment in the five minutes that -- that you spent going past the State Hospital that you saw the cannon being fired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I saw it at the time, yes. But the detonation from the cannon can be felt a kilometre away, near to the electrical engineering faculty or near the hotel at Marindvor, even before you reach Holiday Inn, which is the only hotel in Sarajevo, you can feel and sense where the fire came from. And it must have been a dozen times that I was passing through there and hearing detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please answer my question. When you passed the State Hospital, did you ever see the cannon firing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, that was my last sentence where I told you that I saw that a dozen time when I was either on my way to the hospital or on my way back from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to intervene once more. My colleague Sachdeva received on several occasions some direct answers, and this was again a situation where a question is repeated three times, a question that has been asked and answered. He said on several occasions that he had seen that and now he has said that on several occasions he could also hear it from a certain distance. But he said on several occasions that he had seen that. After he gave this direct answer again he has been asked the same question, and it was insisted that he answer that question, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, in the last witness's last sentence, which is on -- on the board before says, It must have been a dozen times that I was passing through here and hearing detonations," and you have asked him whether he ever saw the cannon firing. A slight difference. Slight difference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's why I asked the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, witness, can we agree that, just so I can confirm your evidence when you passed the State Hospital, you saw -- in other words you saw a cannon being fired, you saw a weapon being released from the cannon at times when you passed the State Hospital, is that right, you physically saw it with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapon was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Probably shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know, because I wasn't an artillery specialist. During President Tito when I was doing my military service I only had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bearing in mind he said probably, Mr. Sachdeva. I presume he had a reason for answering that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, where was this cannon located when you saw it being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: It was located within the perimeter of the hospital, perhaps some 20 metres away from the gate to that perimeter out in an open space. It seems that this was done deliberately, so that somebody from the hill might see the cannon, and it was a sort of provocation. It served to provoke them to shoot at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it was fired, as you say, from an open space where it could be seen, not only from persons in the hills but also other persons that may have been milling around the hospital at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Well, they were probably not provoking the persons milling around the hospital. They were provoking the Serbs on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that's what I'm something, sir, that there were people in the hospital and they would have also seen this cannon being fired from the open space. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many people were manning this cannon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know. I was walking without turning my head back, as I said, out of fear. I was merely passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, was it one person, was it more than one person? Do you have any idea, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: There were two or three of them for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were also aware, sir, that in your time in Sarajevo there was considerable presence of United Nations monitors and United Nations personnel. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I never saw them. I would probably seek help from them. I had heard of them being present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're telling the Court, sir, that in your regular trips through the city, as you've described your route, you never saw a United Nations personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see United Nations APC or a United Nations vehicle, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You never saw United Nations personnel and you never saw a United Nations vehicle, yet you're asking the Court to believe the evidence that you have given that for the five minutes or so that you passed the State Hospital you saw these cannons being fired by -- by the military. Is that what your evidence is, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I said what I knew and what I said was the truth. I can tell you that I never saw any UN personnel or anyone along the route that I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So can you tell the Court how many times did you see the cannon being fired. I want to know the number of times you saw this cannon being fired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I said that I was certain that I saw that ten times, not less for sure. More, I'm not sure. But I heard it so many times, I don't know, countless times, as I was passing in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So when you saw this cannon being fired for ten times, can you give me a date of one of the times that it was fired, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I can't. It was a long time ago, and given all that was going on and that was happening to me, I would be likely to forget as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that -- that you're not telling the truth with respect to your evidence about the cannons. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I am claiming that I'm telling the truth. You can tell me openly that I'm lying. However, I state that I'm telling the truth and I'm abiding by the oath that I took. And this is the first time in -- in my 60 years that I am appearing in a court of law, and I am telling you that I am testifying honestly and truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital, did you -- did you always walk from your place to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Always.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you walked down that road, I take it that you've heard that the road was termed "Sniper Alley"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Vojnicko Polje, in my neighbourhood, was known as the lair of snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you -- did you have to travel past the Holiday Inn when you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: Yes. I told you a moment ago, past the Holiday Inn and then the first building after the Holiday Inn, I turned left to cut the road short, and then I would straight on -- and then I would go straight on to the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, there's five minutes remaining of the time allotted to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On your trips, sir, down this road that you took to the Kosevo Hospital, did you ever notice barricades, containers and other contraptions that were used to protect civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: I was only looking at the containers and barricades. As you pass my company, Cengic Vila, toward Marindvor where barricades were placed on the road toward Grbavica, and it was from those barricades that they fired upon Grbavica and of course Serbs fired upon them from Grbavica. That was the only place where I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so the Serbs fired at the civilians that were passing the barricades. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: If I said that the Muslim army was manning these barricades, was present at these barricades, then I've told you everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will only deal with one matter, which has to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Please. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. May I tender this map, please, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is admitted as P916, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will only be broaching one subject quite briefly. He was showing us the route that he took on his way to the doctor. By your leave, I would like to ask him the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Had it not been for that Croat doctor who helped you to go on sick-leave, would you -- would you have ever taken that route on your way to the hospital? Would you have ever gone on sick-leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, this, in my submission, does not arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does it arise, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question. I will put a different question to him, which arises from cross-examination, although in my view this one also arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to questions by Mr. Sachdeva, you said that from the month of July of 1994 all the way to the end of the conflict once weekly you went for these checkups. Can you tell the Judges why did you have to go and have these checkups once a week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-60
utterances.text: These checkups were mandatory for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that, in my submission, also does not arise out of cross-examination. In fact, the once every seven days was mentioned in examination-in-chief and in my submission that would have been the appropriate time to ask that follow-up question, the logical follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I must have been a very easy going prosecutor in my days, because I can't remember jumping up so frequently to object on these grounds. And so how does this arise now, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you will recall my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva insisting on several times that the number be precisely determined of how many times a month, how many times throughout the period the witness went there but there is one important matter that the witness has to answer to, and this is why did he have to go and have these checkups every week. My learned friend insisted on knowing how many times in total the witness went for these checkups. I believe that there's a very important explanation behind all of this, and I believe the witness should be allowed to explain why he had to go and have all these checkups so frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The frequency is one thing. That was what was the subject of the cross-examination, not the cause for the visit. The Chamber rules that it doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, precisely because he went to have these checkups so often in that period of time, which had been the subject of much examination by the Prosecutor, I believe it would benefit the Trial Chamber to know why the witness had to go for these checkups so often. He was not sick, literally speaking. Well, he was afflicted by psychological problems. He had physical problems but I believe that there was another reason why he had to go there so often, and I do believe the Trial Chamber ought to hear this, and if you're not prepared to change your ruling in any way, then I will have to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not changing the ruling. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no other witness, and it's time for the break, anyhow. So we will adjourn until tomorrow at 2.00 p.m. I should say that we will be monitoring the time being taken the parties very strictly to ensure that we finish at the time that we have agreed to conclude, which is 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of July, 2007, at 2.00 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
